opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few different mechanisms, and it's worth separating them because they have quite different safety implications.

The first is just transfer. A lot of what we've seen is that if you train models hard on things that are easy to check, like math problems with known answers, code that either passes the tests or doesn't, you get general reasoning skills that carry over somewhat into domains where you can't check things as cleanly. The model learns to break problems down, notice its own mistakes, try alternatives. Those habits don't care much whether there's a verifier at the end. So some of the progress on fuzzy tasks comes for free, as a side effect of progress on crisp ones.

The second is that a lot of tasks that look fuzzy are partially verifiable if you're clever about it. You can't check whether a research proposal is good, but you can check whether its citations are real, whether the experiments it describes are runnable, whether its claims are internally consistent. You decompose the fuzzy thing into pieces, some of which you can check, and you lean on those. That gets you surprisingly far, though not all the way.

The third, which is the one I care most about and where the hard problems are, is that eventually you're relying on some form of judgment, whether human judgment or a model's judgment, as the training signal. Once you're there, the worry is that you're optimizing for whatever *looks* good to the judge rather than whatever *is* good. With a crisp verifier, if the model gets reward, it actually solved the problem. With a fuzzy judge, the model can get reward by being persuasive, by telling the judge what they want to hear, by producing something that's hard to find flaws in rather than something without flaws. And the stronger the model gets relative to the judge, the bigger that gap can become.

That's a lot of the motivation behind work on things like debate and scalable oversight more broadly. The idea is: if you can't verify the answer directly, can you set up a process where the model's ability is used to help you evaluate it? In debate, you have two copies of the model argue, and the hope is that it's easier to judge who's winning an argument, especially when one side is trying to point out the flaws in the other, than to judge the answer cold. Whether that actually works is partly an empirical question and partly a theoretical one. There are real obstacles. For example, there are cases where a dishonest debater can make an argument that's hard to refute even though it's wrong, because finding the flaw is computationally harder than making the argument. We've spent a fair amount of time trying to understand when that kind of thing bites and what protocol changes might address it.

So my honest answer is: models will get better at fuzzy tasks, partly through transfer and partly through training against judgments, and the second part is exactly where we need to be careful. The capability will come either way. The question is whether the training signal on fuzzy tasks rewards being right or rewards seeming right, and I don't think that gets solved by default.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using human or model judgment as a training signal, but does not say labs already use model-generated critiques for difficult-to-verify tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes transfer from verifiable tasks and possible judgment-based training, but does not explain that deployment experience lets labs generate training data for progressively less verifiable tasks.

r003.rationale: The response says some fuzzy-task progress comes through transfer and discusses decomposing tasks into checkable parts; it does not argue that enough task-specific training data removes the need for extensive generalization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a sort of standard story here, which is that reinforcement learning has worked spectacularly well on things like maths and code, because you can check the answer. You run the tests, you check the proof, and you get a clean reward signal. And then the question is: what happens when you move to tasks where there isn't a clean signal? Writing a good policy memo, giving research advice, deciding whether a plan is actually sensible.

My honest expectation is that this is going to be harder but not as hard as people sometimes assume, and the reason is that verification is a spectrum rather than a binary. For most fuzzy tasks, you can't verify the final output directly, but you can decompose it. You can ask: is this argument internally consistent? Does it respond to the strongest objection? Would an expert reading this flag something as obviously wrong? Each of those sub-judgements is a bit more checkable than the whole thing. So a lot of the progress I expect is from turning one very fuzzy judgement into many less fuzzy ones.

The second piece is that you can use the models themselves as part of the verification. This is the thing I've spent a lot of time on, with debate and related ideas. If you have two models arguing opposite sides, and a judge who only has to pick which argument is better rather than solve the problem from scratch, you've shifted the burden. The judge's task is easier than the original task. And there are theoretical reasons to think that under the right conditions, honest arguments have an advantage, because a lie has to be defended at every level of detail, and eventually you hit a claim that can be checked.

Now, I want to be careful, because there's a failure mode here that worries me a lot. If your reward for a fuzzy task comes from a model-based judge, and the judge has systematic blind spots, then you're optimising hard against those blind spots. You get outputs that look great to the judge and are subtly worse in reality. That's not hypothetical, we already see mild versions of it with sycophancy, with verbose answers scoring better than concise correct ones. So the capability will probably come, but whether it tracks what we actually want depends on how much work we do on the judging side.

And then the last thing I'd say is that human feedback doesn't go away, it just gets more leveraged. Rather than a human labelling every output, you want humans spot-checking the hardest cases, auditing where the model judges disagree, and training the judges on those. The scarce resource becomes careful human attention on exactly the examples where the automatic process is least trustworthy. If we get that allocation right, I think fuzzy tasks follow the same trajectory as maths, just with more lag and more risk along the way.

r001.rationale: The response describes model-based judging and debate as ways to verify fuzzy tasks, but does not say AI labs already use model-generated critiques as training signals.

r002.rationale: It discusses human spot-checking and training judges, but does not explain that experience from deployed models lets labs generate training data for progressively less verifiable tasks.

r003.rationale: It expects fuzzy-task progress through decomposed judgments and model judging, but does not argue that enough task-specific training data removes the need for extensive generalization beyond training.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the hope is that evaluating an answer is easier than producing it, even when evaluating it isn’t easy in an absolute sense. If you ask me to write a really good essay, that’s hard. If you show me two essays and ask which one makes a more convincing argument, I can often make that judgement without being able to write either one myself. That gives you a training signal.

But there’s a real distinction between learning to do something well and learning to produce something that looks good to the evaluator. If a model makes a subtle error that I can’t spot, or tells me what I want to hear, my feedback can reward the wrong thing.

So one approach is to use models to help with the evaluation itself. You might have one model propose an answer and another point out problems with it. The hope is that checking a particular criticism is easier than judging the whole answer unaided. You’re turning a very fuzzy judgement into a collection of more concrete questions.

I don’t think that makes the problem disappear. You still need to understand when that process actually helps people judge correctly, rather than just generating more persuasive arguments. But it gives us a possible route beyond tasks where we can automatically check the final answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes using one model to critique another as a possible evaluation approach, but does not say AI labs already use those critiques as training signals.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss experience from deployed models being used to generate training data for progressively less verifiable tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that enough task-specific training data can improve fuzzy-task performance without extensive generalization beyond training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that doing a task and judging how well it was done are often quite different in difficulty. You might not be able to write a very good essay yourself, but you can still notice that one argument doesn’t follow, or that a particular claim needs more evidence. So even when we can’t check an answer mechanically, there can be a useful signal to train on.

The concern is that, as models get more capable, they might become better at producing things that look good to us without actually being good. So you need to improve the evaluation process alongside the model. One approach I’ve worked on is debate: have one model propose an answer and another point out problems with it. The hope is that a human can judge a specific disagreement more reliably than they can assess the entire answer unaided.

That doesn’t make every fuzzy task objectively verifiable. There are still questions about what we want, and cases where the judge can be misled. But it gives us a possible way to extend human judgment: use the models to expose the important considerations, rather than requiring the human to discover all of them from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response says critique or debate could provide a useful training signal, but does not say AI labs already use model-generated critiques for this purpose.

r002.rationale: It does not mention experience from deployed models or using that experience to generate training data for progressively less verifiable tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that enough task-specific training data can improve fuzzy-task performance without extensive generalization beyond training.
